summary: Given a string of ()[]{} characters, decide whether every opener is closed by the matching type in the correct nesting order.
mainInsight: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed (last-in, first-out). Push openers; on each closer, the stack top must be its matching opener.
invariant: After processing any prefix, the stack holds exactly the still-unmatched opening brackets in the order they were opened (innermost on top).

approaches.name: Repeated pair removal
approaches.summary: Repeatedly delete '()', '[]' and '{}' substrings until nothing changes; valid iff the string becomes empty.
approaches.interviewRelevance: Mention as a naive idea; the stack is the expected solution.

approaches.name: Stack with closer-to-opener map
approaches.summary: Push openers; for a closer, fail if the stack is empty or its top is not the matching opener; at the end the stack must be empty.
weaknesses: O(n) stack in the worst case

commonMistakes: Forgetting the final 'stack must be empty' check ('((' would pass).
Popping from an empty stack on input like ')'.
Counting brackets per type, which ignores ordering.
edgeCases: Odd length can never be valid.

promptVariants: Which data structure naturally solves bracket matching?
What technique should 'match nested brackets' suggest in an interview?
Which pattern fits Valid Parentheses?
cards.explanation: Nesting means the latest unmatched opener must close first - exactly LIFO order.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Queue: FIFO would match the oldest opener first, which is wrong for nesting.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Two pointers: Matching pairs are not at symmetric positions in general ('()[]{}' is valid).
incorrectOptionExplanations.Union find: There is no connectivity merging, just ordered matching.

promptVariants: Why is a stack the right structure for bracket matching?
Explain the core idea of the Valid Parentheses solution.
cards.answer: Valid nesting means the most recently opened bracket must be closed first. A stack stores unmatched openers with the latest on top, so each closer only needs to compare against the top.
keyPoints: Only the top can match a closer
Closers never need to look deeper
cards.explanation: Any mismatch at the top is immediately an error, since deeper openers are blocked by the innermost one.

promptVariants: What does the stack contain after processing a prefix of the string?
State the loop invariant for the bracket stack.
cards.answer: Exactly the opening brackets that have not been matched yet, in the order opened, with the innermost on top.
cards.explanation: A closer either matches (and removes) the top opener or proves the string invalid.

promptVariants: Why is keeping one counter per bracket type not enough?
What does a counting solution get wrong?
options: Counters ignore nesting: '([)]' balances by count but is invalid
Counters use far more memory than a stack would in total
Counters cannot track more than one kind of bracket at once
Counters are slower than a stack at every single step taken
cards.answer: Counters ignore nesting: '([)]' balances by count but is invalid
cards.explanation: Balanced counts are necessary but not sufficient; order and type interleaving matter.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Counters use far more memory than a stac: Counters use less memory, which is why they are tempting - but wrong.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Counters cannot track more than one kind: You can keep one counter per type; the problem is order.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Counters are slower than a stack at ever: Speed is not the issue; correctness is.

incorrectOptionExplanations.(): A normal valid string; the stack is non-empty when the closer arrives.

incorrectOptionExplanations.{[]}: Valid and always has an opener available for each closer.

promptVariants: After the loop, return True only if the stack is ___.
The final check for '(((' is that the stack must be ___.
cards.explanation: Leftover openers (like '((') are unmatched, so the string is invalid even though no mismatch occurred.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the stack solution: ___
Valid Parentheses runs in ___ time with a stack.
cards.explanation: Each character is pushed or popped at most once, each in O(1).

promptVariants: What is the worst-case extra space, and which input causes it?
When does the bracket stack use the most memory?
options: O(1), because there are only three bracket types
cards.explanation: All openers are pushed and never popped, so the stack grows to n. (Also '((()))' reaches n/2.)

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(1), because there are only three brack: The number of types is constant, but the stack stores one entry per unmatched opener.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n), only for '()()()': In '()()()' the stack never holds more than one element.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(log n) for balanced nesting: Nesting depth can be Θ(n), e.g. '((((....))))'.

promptVariants: Why is `not stack` tested before `stack.pop()`, and what does the `or` guarantee?
Explain the condition `if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]`.
cards.answer: `or` short-circuits: if the stack is empty the pop never executes (so no IndexError) and we return False. Otherwise the popped top is compared with the opener expected for this closer; a mismatch means wrong type/order.
keyPoints: Pop and compare in one step
cards.explanation: The final `return not stack` handles leftover openers.

promptVariants: Why map closers to openers (rather than openers to closers)?
What does a closer-keyed dict give you for free?
options: A key identifies a closer; its value is the opener to match
It makes lookups O(1) while the other direction is O(n)
Openers cannot be used as dictionary keys in Python at all
It lets you avoid the stack for matching the brackets
cards.answer: A key identifies a closer; its value is the opener to match
cards.explanation: Keyed by closer, `ch in pairs` is both the 'is this a closer?' test and the lookup of the expected opener.

incorrectOptionExplanations.It makes lookups O(1) while the other di: Both directions are O(1) hash lookups.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Openers cannot be used as dictionary key: They can; it would simply be less convenient here.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It lets you avoid the stack for matching: The stack is still required to remember unmatched openers.

promptVariants: If len(s) is ___, the string can be rejected immediately.
A quick early exit: strings of ___ length can never be valid.
cards.explanation: Brackets come in pairs, so a valid string has even length.

promptVariants: Describe a non-stack approach and why it is worse.
How could you solve Valid Parentheses with string replacement, and what does it cost?
cards.answer: Repeatedly remove '()', '[]' and '{}' from the string until it stops changing; valid iff it ends empty. Each pass is O(n) and up to n/2 passes are needed, so O(n^2) worst case.
keyPoints: Up to n/2 passes of O(n)
cards.explanation: It works because innermost pairs are always adjacent, but the repeated rescans waste time.
